ideas.title: Order residual-code levels by next-item predictiveness
ideas.motivation: RQ-VAE residual levels are ordered by reconstruction mechanics, not by how useful each level is for predicting what users consume next. A generative recommender that emits a fixed-length SID autoregressively can benefit when the early SID tokens expose the most continuation-relevant distinctions first, particularly under limited context or decoding budget.
ideas.novelty: This leaves the learned item embeddings, codebooks, assignments, and number of tokens untouched; unlike geometry/assignment changes, it permutes the existing level-to-position serialization using only train-split transitions. No transition graph is fed back into tokenizer fitting.
ideas.key_change: After baseline RQ-VAE training and hard assignment, compute a train-only transition-predictiveness score for each code level, then serialize each item's same codes in descending score order. Carry the same global level permutation into Stage 3 SID tokenization; item identity remains one deterministic global tuple.

specification.text: Let c[i,l] be the baseline code for item i at residual level l, and let T[i,j] count adjacent train-sequence transitions i->j (count each sequence adjacency once). For each level l compute S_l = sum_{i,j} T[i,j] * PMI(c[j,l], c[i,all]) / (sum_{i,j} T[i,j] + eps), where c[i,all] is the full source SID tuple; estimate PMI with add-one smoothed counts over training transitions and truncate negative PMI to zero. To avoid self-information, use source-prefix c[i,all] only as conditioning context and score target level c[j,l] by conditional mutual information I(c[j,l]; c[i,all] | c[j,other levels]) (equivalently estimate smoothed train transition contingency tables); sort levels by descending S_l, ties by original level index. Simpler minimally specified estimator: score S_l=I(c[j,l]; c[i,all]) under the empirical train adjacency distribution. Replace emitted tuple (c[i,0],...,c[i,L-1]) by (c[i,pi[0]],...,c[i,pi[L-1]]) with one fixed permutation pi. Train Stage 3 exactly as baseline and compare identical settings; do not use validation/test transitions to choose pi.

ideas.cost_estimate: Tokenizer fitting and each of the 24 Stage 3 steps are unchanged. One CPU pass over train adjacencies and L small contingency tables (at most 24,556 transitions per epoch-equivalent pass; one-time computation), negligible versus 3,000 GPU epochs; per-step additional cost is exactly zero.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: The train-only predictive ordering improves Stage 3 test_R@10 over 0.06335 using the identical Stage 3 recipe, and its gain is larger than the baseline ordering when measuring next-token accuracy at the first SID position. If the early-position token accuracy and final recall do not improve, or recall falls despite token accuracy gain, the serialization change is not worth keeping.
ideas.risks: Code levels may be redundant or have near-tied scores, making the ordering noisy; transition statistics may overfit popular items and fail to generalize. Stage 3 may already model all SID positions equally well, in which case reordering does not improve ranking. Ensure the inverse mapping and every export/inference path use the same fixed permutation.

ideas.title: Whiten embedding axes by train-item covariance before quantization
ideas.motivation: A few high-variance embedding directions can dominate Euclidean residual assignment even when those directions reflect broad metadata/style variation rather than distinctions that help separate candidate items. This can waste successive codebooks modeling the same dominant axes and leave finer discriminative structure unresolved.
ideas.novelty: This is a fixed, train-only coordinate preconditioner of the input space, not a new curved geometry, balanced assignment, behavior auxiliary target, or learned graph residual. The ordinary RQ-VAE objective, architecture, and hard nearest-code assignment remain unchanged in the transformed coordinates.
ideas.key_change: Estimate a shrinkage covariance from training-item embeddings once, transform embeddings by its inverse square root before RQ-VAE training, and keep that transform fixed. Quantize transformed vectors with the baseline model and assign every item one global SID as usual.

specification.text: Given train item embeddings x_i in R^d, compute mean mu and covariance Sigma=(1/N)sum_i (x_i-mu)(x_i-mu)^T. Use shrinkage Sigma_s=(1-rho)Sigma+rho*(tr(Sigma)/d)I with rho=0.1, eigendecompose Sigma_s=U diag(s) U^T, and define A=U diag(1/sqrt(max(s_k, 0.01*mean(s)))) U^T. Transform all train item vectors as y_i=A(x_i-mu); fit the unmodified baseline RQ-VAE on y_i. Apply the same frozen mu,A to validation/test item embeddings before SID assignment. Export the exact single hard code tuple per item; no split-specific fitting or per-user code variant.

ideas.cost_estimate: One covariance/eigendecomposition costs O(N*d^2+d^3) once; for the baseline embedding dimension (typically a few hundred), this is seconds to minutes on CPU and small relative to tokenizer training. Transform adds O(B*d^2) per step for batch B if implemented naively, or precompute y_i once and index it, yielding effectively zero added per-step cost across 24 steps/epoch and 3,000 epochs. No change to RQ-VAE compute thereafter.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: At least one identical Stage 3 run using whitened-coordinate SIDs exceeds test_R@10 0.06335, with improvement concentrated among items whose baseline embedding error aligns with top-variance axes. Log per-axis variance captured by residual codebooks and compare next-item recall for those items; if whitening changes the geometry but neither that slice nor overall recall improves, reject it.
ideas.risks: Embedding anisotropy may encode real useful semantic structure, and whitening can amplify low-variance noise despite shrinkage; it may also distort distances relevant to the pretrained embedding space. Covariance must be estimated over training items only, and identical normalization and frozen transform must be used for every item at assignment time.
